headline: The surprising reason some people sleep better than others
author: Shannon Osaka

paragraphs.text: In the United States, wealth and socioeconomic status is a great determiner of health. The top 1 percent of male income earners, for example, live on average 15 years longer than the bottom 1 percent. (For women, the difference is around 10 years.) The reasons for this divide are legion: Access to medical care, food and housing insecurity, stress and environmental pollution.
But there’s another significant difference between the wealthy and the poor, a new study shows: quality and quantity of sleep.

A new study in the journal JAMA Network Open this month of more than 12,000 participants found sleep duration is strongly associated with economic stability; participants with greater economic stability had much less variability in their amount of sleep and also slept more total minutes per night.

The research affirms other analyses that have found a strong connection between people’s income and amount of sleep. One analysis by the Centers for Disease Control in 2015 found that 35 percent of people with incomes below the federal poverty level slept less than six hours per night, compared to 27 percent with family incomes greater than three times the federal poverty level.

Dayna Johnson, a professor of epidemiology at Emory University and one of the authors of the new study, said that poor sleep can damage many systems of the body. “Poor sleep affects our lives, our livelihoods,” she said. “It’s associated with worse cardiovascular health, obesity, hypertension, diabetes. There’s also emerging data that it’s associated with a higher risk of cancer.”

Many studies rely on self-reported measures of sleep, which can be skewed by what participants think is an appropriate amount of sleep to report. But the new analysis drew data from wearable technology, like a Fitbit, to track the amount of sleep participants got with precision.

Researchers say there many reasons low socioeconomic status can make it difficult to sleep reliably. “Sleep is an opponent process to vigilance,” said Lauren Hale, a professor of preventive medicine at Stony Brook University who was not involved in the study. “You need to turn off at night. You can’t do that if you’re worried about what’s my kid going to eat tomorrow, how am I going to get to my job.”

Higher levels of air pollution can also make patients more likely to develop sleep apnea, which in turn erodes sleep quality. Low-income families also may be more likely to live in an area with a lot of noise, or work jobs that require variable hours.

Not every study, however, has found that higher incomes lead to better sleep. Some economists have found that higher wages can actually lead to less sleep, as people trade in hours of sleep for more hours of work.

But sleep researchers say that across various studies, people of very low incomes or living in poverty are likely to sleep less, endangering their health. “Poverty leads you to be in a situation where sleep becomes difficult,” said Michael Grandner, director of the sleep and health research program at the University of Arizona.

The differences in sleep can have serious effects on mortality. Research has shown that people who sleep less than seven hours a night have a 14 percent higher risk of dying prematurely than people who sleep seven to eight hours. Interestingly, people who sleep more than nine hours a night have also been found to have higher mortality risks, likely due to a correlation with chronic illness and higher amounts of sleep.

Grandner says that lack of consistent, stable sleep creates a long-term debt from which your body has to recover. He has a few suggestions for people who feel that they chronically don’t get enough sleep. He advises that people try to at least have a regular schedule, which will help the body recover even if the amount of sleep is insufficient. If you’re struggling to fall asleep, he adds, it’s better to get up and do something else, instead of training your body that being in bed is stressful.
“You miss an oil change for a few miles, and your car won’t break down on the side of the road,” he said. “But you continue to ignore maintenance and you’re courting danger.”
